Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: John, a 42-year-old male of Oceania descent, is an electrician who has been grappling with profound distress following a violent assault he experienced at his workplace. The incident occurred late one evening around 9 PM, and since then, the specific time of day triggers intense feelings of detachment for John. He begins to feel as if he's in another world or that everything around him seems unreal, which is compounded by sudden sounds, like doors slamming. John's symptoms have evolved into a complex pattern over the past few months. On days when the assault feels particularly vivid and overwhelming, he turns to his phone, immersing himself in games or scrolling through social media for hours on end. He uses this screen time as an escape from the thoughts that constantly threaten to overwhelm him. Similarly, alcohol has become a coping mechanism; it numbs the pain but only temporarily. John avoids watching television or reading about events similar to his assault, fearing these would trigger vivid flashbacks. One evening around 9 PM, John was at home when he heard the door slam shut with force. This sound immediately transported him back to the moment of the assault. He began to feel detached and unreal, a dissociative feeling that made it difficult for him to focus on anything else. To cope with this overwhelming sensation, he reached for his phone, spending hours playing games to distract himself from the intrusive memories. John’s guilt deepens every time he recalls the event; he feels responsible for what happened. He remembers only snapshots of the assault, fragmented moments that seem like still pictures in his mind. Each recall brings intense feelings of guilt and a sense that he is missing crucial pieces of information about the incident. This incompleteness makes him feel vulnerable and exposed. His negative appraisals have taken root deeply: John believes that if someone else were in his shoes, they wouldn't have ended up in such a situation. He feels that something intrinsic to who he is made him susceptible to this assault, leading him to question whether he can ever trust himself or the world around him again. This hopelessness weighs heavily on him; it seems like there’s no future ahead. The negative appraisals intensify his sense of threat. When someone touches him unexpectedly, he reacts with alarm, convinced that danger could strike at any moment. He avoids unfamiliar places because assessing potential threats is too exhausting and anxiety-inducing. Each time he feels detached or experiences vivid memories, he turns to his phone or alcohol for relief. John’s partner has noticed a significant change in him over the past few months. He has become more isolated and distant, spending less time with friends and family. His work as an electrician is also affected; he often finds it hard to concentrate on tasks, especially when there are sudden movements around him or unexpected sounds. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has led John to seek help. What finally brought him to therapy was the realization that his coping mechanisms were no longer effective and that he was spiraling further into a state of hopelessness. He is most afraid of being trapped in this cycle of fear and detachment, but he also hopes for relief from the overwhelming anxiety and guilt that have taken over his life. John’s story illustrates how the traumatic event has woven deeply into his daily existence, influencing his thoughts, feelings, and behaviors in a self-reinforcing loop. The triggers he experiences at specific times or through sudden sounds lead him to employ maladaptive strategies like screen time and alcohol use, which further entrench his negative appraisals and sense of threat. This cycle has left John feeling isolated and uncertain about the future, but with therapy, he hopes to break free from this debilitating pattern.
